title: Introduction to Pointers - Section Header
summary: Section divider slide marking the beginning of the Introduction to Pointers section of the lecture.
main_text: This is a section header slide that introduces the topic of pointers. The upcoming slides will cover what pointers are, why they are needed, and how they relate to pass-by-reference in C/C++.
notes_text: This section will review pass-by-value vs. pass-by-reference behavior and motivate the need for pointers to enable pass-by-reference for scalar variables.

title: Recall: Pass-by-Reference vs Pass-by-Value
summary: Reviews how scalar variables are passed by value (copies) while arrays are passed by reference (addresses/links) in C/C++.
main_text: Single (scalar) variables are passed-by-value in C/C++. Copies are passed, like email attachments. Arrays are passed-by-reference. Links (addresses) are passed, like a link to a shared doc. Changes are made to the original argument, not a copy. The array need not be returned since the function is modifying the original. For scalar arguments, the caller sends a copy to the callee, and a return value is needed to communicate results back. For array arguments, the caller sends a link/address to the callee, allowing the callee to directly modify the original data.
notes_text: The email attachment vs. shared document link analogy is key: pass-by-value creates an independent copy (attachment), while pass-by-reference shares the same data (shared link). This distinction is fundamental to understanding why pointers are needed for scalar variables.

images.description: Two diagrams comparing scalar and array argument passing. Left side shows scalar arguments: caller sends a copy (step 1) and callee returns a value (step 2). Right side shows array arguments: caller sends a link/address (step 1) directly to the callee.

title: Scalar Arguments: Pass-by-Value
summary: Demonstrates that scalar arguments are passed by value, meaning changes to the copy in the callee are not visible to the caller.
main_text: Scalar (single) arguments are passed-by-value (i.e. a copy is passed). Any changes to the copy made by the function (e.g. dec()) ARE NOT VISIBLE to the caller (i.e. main()). Example code: void dec(int); is the prototype. In main(), int y = 3; then dec(y); is called, and cout << y << endl; still prints 3 because y was not changed. In dec(int y), y--; only modifies the local copy. The stack area of RAM shows that dec has its own copy of y at address 0xbf0 with value 2, while main's y at address 0xbf8 still holds 3. Each function has its own copy of the variable.
notes_text: The key insight is that the callee gets its own separate copy of the variable on the stack. The stack diagram clearly shows two different memory locations for y, each in a different function's stack frame. The return link stores the address to return to after the function completes.

images.description: Stack diagram showing two stack frames: dec's frame at 0xbf0 with y=2 and return link, and main's frame at 0xbf8 with y=3 and return link. Demonstrates that each function has its own copy of y.

title: Array Arguments: Pass-by-Reference
summary: Shows that arrays are passed by reference, meaning the address is copied and changes in the callee ARE visible to the caller.
main_text: Array arguments are passed-by-reference (i.e. a link/address is passed). Any changes made by the function (e.g. init()) ARE VISIBLE to the caller (i.e. main()). The code shows: void init(int data[], int size); and int sum(int data[], int size); prototypes. In main(), int vals[100] and mysum = 0 are declared. init(vals, 100) is called followed by mysum = sum(vals, 100). The init function: void init(int data[], int size) { for(int i=0; i < size; i++) { data[i] = 5; } }. The stack shows init's frame where data holds 7420 (the address of vals[0] in main). Step 1: We copy the address as init()'s argument, not the values. Step 2: The address allows init() to access the original data in main().
notes_text: The memory diagram shows that init's data parameter at address 7404 contains the value 7420, which is the starting address of the vals array in main's stack frame. This is why changes to data[i] inside init actually modify vals[i] in main. The array name evaluates to the starting address of the array.

images.description: Stack memory diagram showing init's stack frame with data=7420 (address of vals array) and main's stack frame with vals[0] through vals[99] starting at address 7420. Arrows show how init accesses main's data through the address.

title: Can We Pass Scalars By Reference?
summary: Poses the motivating question: can we pass scalar variable addresses to functions to enable modification? Answer: yes, using pointers.
main_text: Can we somehow pass the link/address of a scalar (single) argument so that it can be used to change the original variable back in the caller function? YES!!! Using pointers! Pointers are just variables that store addresses (links). This slide introduces the key motivation for pointers: enabling pass-by-reference behavior for scalar variables, which normally are passed by value in C/C++.
notes_text: This is the pivotal slide that connects the concept of pass-by-reference (which students already understand for arrays) to the new concept of pointers. The key insight is that if we can get and pass the address of a scalar variable, we can achieve the same effect as array pass-by-reference.

title: Pass-by-(Pointer) Reference
summary: Introduces the address-of (&) and dereference (*) operators to enable pass-by-reference for scalars using pointers.
main_text: To GET a link (i.e. address/pointer) to a scalar variable, use the address-of (&) operator. We get links to arrays by just using their name. To STORE a link (i.e. address/pointer) to data of type T, make a variable/argument of type T* (a pointer to a T). Use the dereference (*) operator to change the data at the link/address (being pointed to). Example: void dec(int); prototype becomes void dec(int* ptr). In main(): int y = 3; dec(&y); cout << y << endl; // prints 2. In dec(int* ptr): *ptr = *ptr - 1; // or (*ptr)--;. The stack shows dec's ptr at 0x7bf0 holds value 7bf8 (address of y in main), and *ptr modifies y in main from 3 to 2.
notes_text: Three key steps: (1) use & to get the address of a variable, (2) use T* to declare a pointer variable to store that address, (3) use * to dereference the pointer and access/modify the original variable. The stack diagram shows ptr in dec's frame contains 0x7bf8, which is the address of y in main's frame.

images.description: Stack diagram showing dec's frame with ptr=7bf8 and main's frame with y changing from 3 to 2. An arrow from *ptr connects to y in main's frame, showing how dereferencing the pointer accesses the original variable.

title: Pointer Background - Section Header
summary: Section divider slide marking the beginning of the Pointer Background section.
main_text: This is a section header slide that introduces the Pointer Background section. The upcoming slides will cover the conceptual foundation of pointers, including analogies, memory models, and the fundamental concepts needed to understand how pointers work.
notes_text: This section provides the conceptual groundwork for understanding pointers before diving into the syntax and mechanics of using them in C/C++.

title: Recall: Pass-by-Reference Pros and Cons
summary: Uses a Google Doc vs email attachment analogy to explain the tradeoffs of pass-by-reference vs pass-by-value.
main_text: Scenario: You write a paper and include a lot of LARGE images. You need to send it to your teammates. You can use a Google doc and simply e-mail the URL or attach the document/file in the e-mail. What are the pros of each approach? Google Doc (pass-by-reference): Less info to send (send link, not all data). Reference to original (i.e. if original changes, you will see it). Email Attachment (pass-by-value): Can treat the copy as a scratch copy and modify freely. This analogy maps directly to how C/C++ handles argument passing.
notes_text: The Google Doc analogy is particularly useful because it maps to real-world experience. The link is like a pointer (small, just an address), while the attachment is like pass-by-value (full copy). The tradeoff is efficiency (less data to pass) vs. safety (independent copy that can be modified freely).

images.description: Screenshots showing a Google Doc sharing dialog with 'Copy link' button and a Google Doc about Computer Science Courses, illustrating the concept of sharing via link vs. attachment.

title: Reasons To Use Pointers
summary: Lists three main reasons to use pointers: pass-by-reference, dynamic memory allocation, and accessing specific hardware locations.
main_text: Reason 1: Use pointers when you need pass-by-reference (as opposed to pass-by-value), either to: Change a variable (or variables) local to one function in some other function (analogy: a Google-doc link with 'Can Edit' permission), or Avoid making needless copies of data which wastes time (analogy: A Google-doc link with 'Can View' permission, think large arrays). Reason 2: Use pointers when you perform dynamic memory allocation. Reason 3: We need to access a specific hardware location in the computer (not covered in this class, but EE 109/CS 356). This is useful for embedded systems and device programming. All of these will be explained in the following slides.
notes_text: Reason 1 is the primary focus of this unit. Reason 2 (dynamic memory allocation) will be covered in a later unit. Reason 3 (hardware access) is relevant to systems programming courses. The Google Doc permission analogy extends nicely: 'Can Edit' = non-const pointer, 'Can View' = const pointer.

title: Pointer Analogy (1) - Safe Deposit Boxes
summary: Uses a safe deposit box analogy to explain pointers: boxes have numbers (addresses), some hold gold (data), others hold slips with box numbers (pointers).
main_text: Imagine a set of lockers or safe deposit boxes each with a number (just like memory locations have an address). Some boxes contain gold jewelry (data) and other boxes simply hold a slip of paper with a box number written on it (i.e. a pointer to another box). What is stored in one box might be: Box 7: Gold (i.e. data / something valuable like an int, double, etc.). Box 9: The number of another box which contains gold (i.e. box 9 holds a pointer-to some other data). Box 16: The number of another box which contains a number of a box containing gold (i.e. box 16 holds a pointer-to a pointer-to data). Each box has a number to identify it (i.e. an address) and a value inside of it. So do variables in memory. The value of one box might be the address of another box. By changing the number in a box (i.e. the value of a pointer), we can have one location refer to many different locations, in succession.
notes_text: This analogy helps students understand the layered nature of pointers. A pointer is just a box whose contents happen to be the number of another box. A pointer-to-a-pointer is a box whose contents are the number of a box that itself contains the number of yet another box. The grid diagram shows 18 boxes (0-17) each with a number identifier and a value inside.

images.description: Photo of safe deposit boxes and a grid of 18 numbered boxes (0-17) each containing a value. Box numbers represent addresses and values inside represent data or pointers to other boxes.

title: Pointer Analogy (2) - Ambiguity Without Types
summary: Shows that without type information, you cannot distinguish whether a box stores data, a pointer, or a pointer to a pointer.
main_text: But what if rather than gold or other obvious data, the 'valuable objects' were simply slips of papers with numbers? Would you be able to distinguish whether a box is storing data, a pointer, or even a pointer to a pointer? And if it is storing a pointer, would you know whether it is pointing at just 1 data element or an array of data elements? The answer to both questions is no -- you cannot tell just by looking at the contents. This motivates why we need pointer types in C/C++ to tell us how to interpret the contents of a memory location.
notes_text: This is a crucial conceptual point: memory itself does not distinguish between data and pointers. All values in memory are just numbers (bit patterns). The type system in C/C++ provides the context needed to interpret whether a value is data or an address. This is why pointer types exist.

images.description: Photo of safe deposit boxes and a grid of 18 boxes (0-17) with numeric values, illustrating that without type information all values look the same and you cannot distinguish data from pointers.

title: Pointer Analogy (3) - Why We Need Pointer Types
summary: Explains that pointer types (int*, char*, int**) tell us how to interpret memory contents -- whether it is data, a pointer, or a pointer to a pointer.
main_text: Would you be able to distinguish whether a box is storing: data, a pointer, or even a pointer to a pointer? No! This is why we need pointer types. Pointer types (e.g. int* or char*) tell us how to interpret the contents of the variable. Is it data or a pointer, and if it is a pointer what kind of data we will find when we follow (dereference) the pointer (e.g. int or char). As the programmer, we must always keep these types in mind to use the variable correctly. The diagram shows boxes labeled with types: char (data), char* (pointer to char), int (data), int* (pointer to int), int** (pointer to pointer to int).
notes_text: The type system is essential for safe pointer usage. An int* tells us two things: (1) this variable holds an address, and (2) at that address we will find an int. An int** tells us this variable holds an address of another variable that itself holds an address of an int. Type mismatches (e.g. assigning a char address to an int*) are errors.

images.description: Grid of numbered boxes with type annotations showing how different types (char, int, int*, char*, int**) label the same numeric contents to indicate how to interpret them.

title: Reading Pointer Types Right-to-Left
summary: Teaches how to read pointer type declarations from right-to-left, reading each * as 'pointer to a'.
main_text: To understand a type, read it from right-to-left and each * as 'pointer to a'. Example: int** is read as 'A pointer to a pointer to an int'. This right-to-left reading technique helps decode complex pointer declarations. For example: int* is 'a pointer to an int', double* is 'a pointer to a double', char** is 'a pointer to a pointer to a char'. This technique becomes even more useful with more complex type declarations.
notes_text: The right-to-left reading rule is a practical technique that students should memorize. It works for simple and complex pointer types. For declarations with const, the rule extends: const int* reads as 'a pointer to a const int' (cannot modify what is pointed to), while int* const reads as 'a const pointer to an int' (cannot change where it points).

images.description: Diagram showing int** with an arrow pointing left, and the reading 'A pointer to a pointer to an int' with color-coded segments matching each part of the type.

title: Pointers Overview
summary: Defines pointers as variables storing addresses of other variables, notes all pointers are 8 bytes on 64-bit systems, and gives real-world analogies.
main_text: Pointers are variables that store the address of some other variable in memory. All pointers are 8 bytes (64-bits in a modern 64-bit OS). Pointers are references to other 'things' which can be: data (i.e. ints, chars, doubles) or other pointers. We can change what they point at so that with one pointer we can reference many variables. The concept of a pointer is very common and used in many places in everyday life. Excel workbook has cell names we can use to reference the data (=A1 means get data in A1). URLs (www.usc.edu is a pointer to a physical HTML file on some server) and can be used in any other page to 'point to' USC's website. The memory diagram shows ptr1 (int*) at address 73a8 containing 00000000, ptr2 (double*) at 73b0 containing 000073b8, int a at 73b8 containing 108, and double z at 73bc containing -2.25.
notes_text: Key facts: (1) ALL pointers are the same size (8 bytes on 64-bit systems) regardless of what they point to -- an int* and a double* are both 8 bytes because they store addresses, not data. (2) Pointers can reference data or other pointers. (3) The everyday analogies (Excel cell references, URLs) help ground the abstract concept in familiar territory.

images.description: Memory diagram showing addresses and data: ptr1 (int*) at 73a8, ptr2 (double*) at 73b0 pointing to address 73b8, int a=108 at 73b8, and double z=-2.25 at 73bc.

title: Pointer Basics - Section Header
summary: Section divider introducing the Pointer Basics section. Prerequisites listed: Data Sizes, Computer Memory.
main_text: This is a section header for Pointer Basics. Prerequisites for this section include understanding Data Sizes and Computer Memory. The upcoming slides will cover the fundamental C++ syntax and operations for working with pointers, including declaring pointer variables, using the address-of (&) operator, and using the dereference (*) operator.
notes_text: Students should already understand how different data types have different sizes (int = 4 bytes, double = 8 bytes, char = 1 byte) and how variables are stored in memory at specific addresses. These concepts are essential for understanding pointer arithmetic later.

title: C++ Pointer Operators: & and * (Google Doc Analogy)
summary: Introduces the two pointer operators using a Google Doc analogy: & gets a link (address-of), * follows the link (dereference).
main_text: Two operators are used to manipulate pointers (i.e. addresses) in C/C++. The & (address-of op) gets a link/pointer, like getting a shareable link from a Google Doc (right-click, 'Get link'). The * (dereference op) follows the link/pointer, like clicking on a Google Doc link to open the document. Notice: the dereference * is not the binary * operator (e.g. multiply a*b). It is the unary * operator (e.g. *a). The visual shows a Google Doc file list with a 'Get link' option (representing &) and a link being clicked to navigate to the document (representing *).
notes_text: The Google Doc analogy makes the abstract concepts concrete: & is like right-clicking a file and selecting 'Get link' to obtain a shareable URL, while * is like clicking that URL to navigate to and interact with the actual document. The distinction between unary * (dereference) and binary * (multiplication) is important to avoid confusion.

images.description: Screenshots of Google Docs interface showing the 'Get link' option in a file context menu (representing &) and clicking a link URL to open a document (representing *).

title: C++ Pointer Operators: & and * (Technical Details)
summary: Formally defines & as evaluating to the address of a variable and * as evaluating to the data at the address stored in a pointer.
main_text: Two operators are used to manipulate pointers (i.e. addresses) in C/C++. The & (address-of op) gets a link/pointer: &<variable> evaluates to the 'address-of' <variable>. Example: &variable => address/pointer. Given int x at address 73a8 with value 42, &x => 73a8. The * (dereference op) follows the link/pointer: *<pointer> evaluates to the data pointed to by <pointer> (data at the address given by <pointer>). Example: *pointer => variable value. *73a8 => x (i.e. 42). So & takes a variable and produces its address, while * takes an address and produces the value stored there.
notes_text: The formal definitions are: & maps variable -> address, and * maps address -> value. These are inverse operations. The memory diagram shows int x with value 42 at address 73a8, so &x produces 73a8 and *73a8 produces 42 (which is x).

images.description: Memory diagram showing int x = 42 at address 73a8, with &x => 73a8 and *73a8 => x (i.e. 42) illustrated in separate boxes.

title: Inverse Operations: & and *
summary: Demonstrates that & and * are inverse operations: &variable gives the address, *pointer gives the value, and *(&variable) gives back the variable.
main_text: The & and * are inverse operations. &variable => address/pointer. *pointer => variable value. *(&variable) => variable (applying & then * gets you back to the original). Example: int x = 42; then *&x is the same as just typing x. This is a 'useless example' because you would never write *&x in practice -- you would just use x directly. But it demonstrates that & and * cancel each other out. The visual shows the Google Doc analogy: & is like getting a link, * is like following the link back to the document.
notes_text: Understanding that & and * are inverses is important for reasoning about pointer expressions. While *&x is trivially equivalent to x, understanding this inverse relationship helps when dealing with more complex expressions involving multiple levels of indirection. The code example 'int x = 42; *&x // same as just typing, x' reinforces this concept.

images.description: Google Doc analogy showing & = get a link and * = follow the link, with a memory diagram of int x = 42 at address 73a8, and code showing *&x is equivalent to x.

title: Getting a Link/Pointer with the & Operator
summary: Shows how declaring variables allocates memory at specific addresses, and the & operator retrieves those addresses.
main_text: When a variable is declared, memory is allocated for it. Its starting location in memory is its address. Given: int x = 30; char y = 'a'; double z = 3.75; int dat[2] = {103,42}; To generate a pointer, use the & operator (Tip: Read '&x' as 'address of x'). &x => 73a8 (address of int x which holds 30), &y => 73ac (address of char y which holds 97/'a'), &z => 73b0 (address of double z which holds 3.75), &dat[0] => 73b8 (address of first element), &dat[1] => 73bc (address of second element), dat => 73b8 (array name evaluates to address of first element). But what would we do with these pointers? We need POINTER variables to store and manipulate these addresses. The diagram also shows individual byte addresses within a 4-byte integer at address 73ac: bytes 73ac, 73ad, 73ae, 73af containing 97, 00, 00, 00.
notes_text: Key observations: (1) Each variable type occupies a different amount of memory: int = 4 bytes, char = 1 byte (but may be padded), double = 8 bytes. (2) An array name by itself evaluates to the address of its first element, so dat and &dat[0] give the same value. (3) The byte-level view shows that the value 97 (ASCII 'a') is stored in little-endian format.

images.description: Memory layout diagram showing variables at specific addresses: x=30 at 73a8, y='a' at 73ac, z=3.75 at 73b0-73b7, dat[0]=103 at 73b8, dat[1]=42 at 73bc. Also shows byte-level view of address 73ac.

title: Steps To Using Pointers
summary: Outlines three steps to use pointers: have a variable with real data, declare a pointer variable, get the link with &, and dereference with *.
main_text: Step 1: Have a variable storing REAL data. You can't use pointers without something to point to (create a variable of some type, T var). Note: We use T as a placeholder for ANY type. Example: int x = 42; Step 2: Declare a pointer variable to store the link. To point to a variable of type T, declare a variable of type T* (e.g. T* ptr;). Example: int x = 42; int* p; Step 3: Get the Link. Generate the pointer/link to the ACTUAL variable using & operator (&var). Example: int x = 42; int* p; p = &x; Step 4: Dereference (Use the Link). Follow the link to view or edit the variable using the * operator (*pvar). Example: int x = 42; int* p; p = &x; *p += 1; // x is now 43. The visual uses Google Doc icons: document icon for data, link icon for pointer, and clicking a URL for dereference.
notes_text: These four steps form a template that students should follow every time they use pointers: (1) Create data, (2) Declare pointer, (3) Assign address to pointer, (4) Dereference to use. Skipping step 3 (forgetting to initialize the pointer) leads to undefined behavior and crashes.

images.description: Visual progression showing four steps of using pointers with Google Doc icons: document (data), link chain (pointer), Copy link button (get address), and clicking URL (dereference), alongside corresponding C++ code.

title: Pointer Variables and their Declaration
summary: Shows how to declare pointer variables using T* syntax, explains type matching rules, and demonstrates initialization with addresses.
main_text: Data variable declarations: int x = 30; char y = 'a'; double z = 3.75; int dat[2] = {103,42}; We can now declare pointer variables that don't store data but the addresses of data. To declare a pointer, include a * after the type (e.g. int*, which is read 'pointer to (an) int(s)'). That variable can then store pointers to (addresses of) the given type (e.g. int). Examples: int *ptr1 = &x; // ptr1 = 0x73a8. double* ptr2 = &z; // ptr2 = 0x73b0. int* ptr3 = &y; // Error! Type mismatch. Important notes: 1. Pointers should ONLY store the addresses of variables of its declared type (int* pointers should only point at ints, not chars). 2. Best to immediately initialize a pointer with the address of some variable, rather than leave it uninitialized. 3. Where the * is in the declaration (i.e. next to the type or variable name) does not matter (e.g. int* ptr1 or int *ptr1).
notes_text: The memory diagram shows ptr1 at 73c0 containing 000073a8 (address of x) and ptr2 at 73c4 containing 000073b0 (address of z). The arrow labeled 'Pointer = link' connects ptr1 to x. Type safety is enforced: int* ptr3 = &y is an error because y is a char, not an int.

images.description: Memory layout showing data variables (x, y, z, dat) and pointer variables (ptr1 pointing to x, ptr2 pointing to z) with addresses and values. Shows the connection between pointers and their targets.

title: Dereferencing Pointer Variables
summary: Demonstrates using the * operator to access and modify data through pointer variables, including reading and writing through dereferenced pointers.
main_text: Data variable declarations: int x = 30; char y = 'a'; double z = 3.75; int dat[2] = {103,42}; We can declare pointer variables that store addresses of other variables: int *ptr1 = &x; // ptr1 = 0x73a8. double* ptr2 = &z; // ptr2 = 0x73b0. We can access the data whose address is stored in a pointer variable by dereferencing it using the * operator. *ptr can be read as 'get/set the data at the address stored in ptr'. Examples: dat[1] = *ptr1 + 5; // dat[1] = 30 + 5 = 35. *ptr2 = *ptr2 - 1.25; // z = 3.75 - 1.25 = 2.5. It may be confusing but notice the * appears both in the declaration and in the dereference expression. Context is important to distinguish. The memory diagram shows *ptr1 following the arrow from ptr1 to x, and *ptr2 following from ptr2 to z.
notes_text: The dual meaning of * is a common source of confusion: in a declaration (int *ptr1), * indicates ptr1 is a pointer; in an expression (*ptr1 + 5), * dereferences the pointer to get the value. Context determines which meaning applies. After the operations shown, dat[1] changes from 42 to 35, and z changes from 3.75 to 2.5.

images.description: Memory diagram showing ptr1 at 73c0 pointing to x at 73a8, and ptr2 at 73c4 pointing to z at 73b4. Arrows labeled *ptr1 and *ptr2 show the dereference paths. Values update after operations.

title: Pointer Details: Placement, Type Safety, and Uninitialized Pointers
summary: Covers three important pointer details: * placement in declarations doesn't matter, type matching is required, and uninitialized pointers cause crashes.
main_text: Where you type the * in the declaration does not matter! int* ptr1 ..or.. int *ptr1 // Equivalent. int* variables can only store addresses of integers, double* variables can only store addresses of doubles. Example error: double z=4.0; int* ptr1 = &z; // ERROR: Not Allowed! An int* and double* are apples and oranges (completely different). Beware of uninitialized pointers. Dereferencing them usually crashes the program! Example: int* ptr1; // Garbage address. *ptr1 = 42; // Crash! The pointer contains a random garbage value that is almost certainly not a valid memory location you own.
notes_text: Three critical rules: (1) Asterisk placement is flexible in single declarations but be careful with multiple declarations on one line (int* a, b; makes a a pointer but b a regular int). (2) Type safety prevents accidentally interpreting memory incorrectly (reading 4 bytes of a double as an int would give nonsense). (3) Always initialize pointers -- uninitialized pointer dereference is undefined behavior and a common source of segfaults.

title: Cutting through the Syntax: Declaration vs Dereference
summary: Provides a clear rule to distinguish declaration from dereference: * after a type declares a pointer, * in an expression dereferences.
main_text: Rule: * after a type = declare/allocate a pointer variable (step 2: Pointer). * in an expression/assignment = dereference (step 4: use/dereference). The table shows examples: 'char *p' is declaring a pointer (checkmark in declaring column). 'x = *p + 1' is de-referencing a pointer (checkmark in de-referencing column). 'int* ptr' is declaring a pointer. '*ptr = 5' is de-referencing. '(*ptr)++' is de-referencing. 'char* p1[10];' is declaring (an array of 10 char pointers). Helpful tip to understand syntax: We declare a pointer as 'int *ptr' because when we dereference it as *ptr, we get an int. Similarly, 'char *p' is a declaration of a pointer and thus, *p yields a char.
notes_text: The mnemonic is powerful: 'int *ptr' means that the expression *ptr has type int. This connects the declaration syntax to the usage syntax. The table format helps students practice identifying which usage of * they are seeing. Note that char* p1[10] declares an array of 10 char pointers, not a pointer to an array.

images.description: Table with two columns (Declaring a pointer, De-referencing a pointer) and rows showing different uses of * with checkmarks indicating which column each example falls under.

title: Assigning to Pointer Variables and Re-pointing
summary: Shows that pointers can be reassigned to point to different variables, and demonstrates multiple dereference operations.
main_text: Data variable declarations: int x = 30; char y = 'a'; double z = 3.75; int dat[2] = {103,42}; Declaring pointer variables and setting them with addresses (using &): int *ptr1 = &x; // ptr1 = 0x73a8. double* ptr2 = &z; // ptr2 = 0x73b0. Dereferencing pointer variables (using *) to get data pointed to: dat[1] = *ptr1 + 5; // dat[1] = 35. *ptr2 = *ptr2 - 1.25; // z = 2.5. We can change what variable the pointer references by assigning a new address to it and dereference the pointer as many times as we like: ptr1 = &dat[1]; then int a = *ptr1 % 10; // a = 35 % 10 = 5 after exec. ptr1 = dat; // why is & not needed? Because array name IS a pointer. *ptr1 += 1; // dat[0] = 103 + 1 = 104. *ptr2 = *ptr1 - *ptr2; // z = 104 - 2.5 = 101.5. The memory diagram shows ptr1 being reassigned from pointing to x to pointing to dat[1] and then to dat[0].
notes_text: Key insight: ptr1 = dat works without & because an array name already evaluates to the address of its first element. This is equivalent to ptr1 = &dat[0]. Pointers are versatile because they can be reassigned -- one pointer variable can reference different data at different times during program execution.

images.description: Memory diagram showing data variables and pointers, with arrows showing ptr1 being reassigned from x to dat[1] to dat, and ptr2 pointing to z. Updated values shown after each operation.

title: Skill: Drawing Data Diagrams (Blank)
summary: Introduces the skill of drawing data diagrams for pointer tracing exercises, with a practice problem from the textbook.
main_text: Though painful, it is helpful to draw out relevant data diagrams, especially when pointers are involved. Instructions: Draw a table with a column for each variable (or just a box for each variable). Label the column header with the variable name and a made-up address. Use whatever number is easiest for your address: @100, @500, etc. Annotate the variable values as you evaluate each line of code. Practice problem from DS Malik Textbook, Chapter 13, Question 6: int x, y; int *p = &x; int* q = &y; x = 35; y = 46; p = q; *p = 78; cout << x << " " << y << endl; cout << *p << " " << *q << endl; The diagram shows variables x at address 600, y at 700, p at 800, and q at 900 with blank boxes to fill in.
notes_text: Drawing data diagrams is an essential skill for understanding pointer code. Students should practice tracing through pointer code line by line, updating the diagram at each step. The made-up addresses (@100, @500) keep the diagrams simple while still conveying the concept of addresses.

images.description: Empty data diagram template with boxes for variables x (at address 600), y (at 700), p (at 800), and q (at 900), with blank spaces to fill in values and output lines.

title: Skill: Drawing Data Diagrams (Solution)
summary: Provides the solution to the data diagram exercise, showing the final output is '35 78' and '78 78'.
main_text: Solution to the tracing exercise: int x, y; (x and y uninitialized, shown as ??). int* p = &x; (p = 600, pointing to x). int* q = &y; (q = 700, pointing to y). x = 35; y = 46; (x = 35, y = 46). p = q; (p now = 700, pointing to y instead of x). *p = 78; (since p now points to y, y changes from 46 to 78, x stays 35). cout << x << " " << y << endl; outputs: 35 78. cout << *p << " " << *q << endl; outputs: 78 78 (both p and q point to y which is 78). The key step is p = q which reassigns p to point to y. After this, *p modifies y (not x). Both *p and *q now evaluate to y's value.
notes_text: The critical line is p = q: this makes p point to the same variable as q (which is y). After this assignment, x is orphaned -- no pointer references it. When *p = 78 executes, it modifies y (which both p and q point to). This is why both *p and *q give 78 in the output. The diagram shows the progression of values through each line of code.

images.description: Completed data diagram showing the progression of values for x, y, p, q through each line of code, with final values x=35, y=78, p=700, q=700, and outputs '35 78' and '78 78'.

title: Pointer Summary
summary: Summarizes pointer fundamentals: declaring with T*, getting addresses with &, assigning to pointers, dereferencing with *, and re-pointing.
main_text: To summarize: We can declare pointer variables to store addresses (not data) using the syntax T* where T is some type (e.g. int *p). We can get the address of some variable using the & operator (e.g. &x, &y). Most often, this would then be assigned to a pointer variable (e.g. p = &x). We can dereference a pointer (i.e. follow a pointer) to get the data from the address it stores by using the * operator (e.g. cout << *p << endl). We can change the address the pointer stores to have it reference some other variable (e.g. p = &z). But why do we need them? Can't we just access x, y, and z directly? Example code: int main() { int x = 103; char y = 'a'; int z = 42; int* p = &x; char *q = &y; *p = 42; cout << *p << endl; p = &z; cout << *p << endl; return 0; }
notes_text: The question 'why do we need pointers if we can access variables directly?' motivates the next section on pass-by-reference. Within a single function, pointers are unnecessary for accessing local variables. Pointers become essential when we need to modify variables across function boundaries, which is exactly what pass-by-reference enables.

title: Pass-by-Reference - Section Header
summary: Section divider introducing the Pass-by-Reference section. Subtitle: Pointer Application 1 - Changing values of another function.
main_text: This section header introduces Pass-by-Reference as Pointer Application 1: Changing values of another function. This is the primary use case for pointers in this unit -- using pointers to enable a called function to modify variables that belong to the calling function.
notes_text: This is the most important application of pointers covered in this unit. It directly addresses the limitation shown earlier: scalar variables are passed by value, so a called function cannot modify the caller's variables without pointers.

title: Steps To Using Pointers for Pass-by-Reference
summary: Shows the complete workflow for using pointers to achieve pass-by-reference: create variable, generate pointer with &, declare pointer parameter, dereference with *.
main_text: The four steps applied to pass-by-reference: Step 1: Variable storing REAL data (T var). Step 2: Generate Pointer/Link with the & operator (&var). Step 3: Pointer parameter (T* pvar). Step 4: Dereference (Use) with the * operator (*pvar). Complete example: // Prototype: void dec(int); In main() (caller): int y = 3; dec(&y); cout << y << endl; // prints 2. In dec(int* ptr) (callee): *ptr = *ptr - 1; // or (*ptr)--;. The visual shows the flow: the data variable y is created, &y generates the link/address, the address is passed to dec's ptr parameter, and *ptr dereferences to access and modify y.
notes_text: This slide ties together all the pointer concepts into the practical pattern for pass-by-reference. The caller uses & to create the pointer, the callee receives it as T*, and the callee uses * to access the original variable. The Google Doc analogy is reinforced: Copy link = &, clicking the link = *.

images.description: Diagram showing the four steps of pointer-based pass-by-reference with Google Doc analogy icons and code example, with arrows connecting the caller's &y to the callee's ptr parameter and *ptr back to y.

title: Swap Two Variables - Pass-by-Value (Blank)
summary: Classic swap example showing that pass-by-value fails: swapping copies in the callee does not affect the caller's variables.
main_text: Classic example of issues with local variables: Write a function to swap two variables. Pass-by-value doesn't work. A copy is made of x,y from main and passed to x,y of swap2(). Swap is performed on the copies. The code: #include <iostream> using namespace std; void swap2(int x, int y); int main() { int x=5,y=7; swap2(x,y); cout << " x=" << x; cout << " y=" << y << endl; } void swap2(int x, int y) { int temp = x; x = y; y = temp; }. The stack shows main's frame with x=5 at 0x7bf0 and y=7 at 0x7bf4. The swap2 frame needs to be filled in to understand why the swap fails.
notes_text: This is a classic CS exercise that demonstrates the fundamental limitation of pass-by-value. Even though swap2 successfully swaps its local copies of x and y, main's x and y remain unchanged because they are separate copies on the stack. The output will be x=5 y=7, not x=7 y=5.

images.description: Stack diagram showing main's frame with x=5 and y=7, with an empty swap2 frame above it to be filled in. Prompts: 'Can you make a memory diagram of what is on the stack for swap2()?'

title: Swap Two Variables - Pass-by-Value (Solution)
summary: Shows the completed stack diagram for the failed swap: swap2's local copies are swapped but main's x and y remain unchanged.
main_text: The completed stack diagram shows why pass-by-value swap fails. swap2's frame: temp=5 at 0x7be0, x starts at 5 then becomes 7 at 0x7be4, y starts at 7 then becomes 5 at 0x7be8, return link at 0x7bec. main's frame: x=5 at 0x7bf0 (unchanged), y=7 at 0x7bf4 (unchanged), return link at 0x7bf8. The swap successfully occurs within swap2's stack frame (its local x goes from 5 to 7, its local y goes from 7 to 5), but main's x and y are completely separate memory locations that are never modified. The output is x=5 y=7, demonstrating the swap failed from main's perspective.
notes_text: The stack diagram makes it visually clear that swap2 has its own copies of x and y at different memory addresses than main's x and y. The swap works perfectly on the copies but has zero effect on the originals. This motivates the need for pointers to share the actual memory locations.

images.description: Completed stack diagram showing swap2's frame with temp=5, x changing from 5 to 7, y changing from 7 to 5, while main's x=5 and y=7 remain unchanged.

title: Swap Two Variables - Pass-by-Reference (Blank)
summary: Shows the correct swap using pointers: addresses of main's variables are passed, allowing swap2 to modify the originals through dereferencing.
main_text: Pass-by-reference (pointers) does work for swapping. Addresses of the actual x,y variables in main are passed. Use those addresses to change those physical memory locations. Code: #include <iostream> using namespace std; void swap2(int* x, int* y); int main() { int x=5,y=7; swap2(&x, &y); cout << " x=" << x; cout << " y=" << y << endl; } void swap2(int* px, int* py) { int temp = *px; *px = *py; *py = temp; }. The stack shows swap2's frame with temp=5 at 0x7be0, px at 0x7be4, py at 0x7be8, and main's x=5 at 0x7bf0, y=7 at 0x7bf4. Students are asked to fill in the values for px and py.
notes_text: The key changes from the pass-by-value version: (1) The function signature changes from int x, int y to int* px, int* py. (2) The call changes from swap2(x,y) to swap2(&x, &y). (3) Inside swap2, all uses of x and y change to *px and *py. These three changes are the template for converting any pass-by-value function to pass-by-reference.

images.description: Stack diagram showing swap2's frame with temp, px, py (px and py values to be filled in), and main's frame with x=5, y=7. Prompt: 'Can you fill in the values for x and y in swap2()?'

title: Swap Two Variables - Pass-by-Reference (Solution)
summary: Completed stack diagram showing the successful swap: px and py hold addresses of main's x and y, dereferencing modifies the originals.
main_text: The completed stack diagram shows the successful pointer-based swap. swap2's frame: temp=5 at 0x7be0, px=0x7bf0 (address of main's x) at 0x7be4, py=0x7bf4 (address of main's y) at 0x7be8, return link at 0x7bec. After execution: main's x changes from 5 to 7 (at 0x7bf0), main's y changes from 7 to 5 (at 0x7bf4). Arrows show *px pointing down to main's x and *py pointing down to main's y. The swap works because: int temp = *px; saves the value at x (5), *px = *py; copies y's value (7) into x, *py = temp; copies saved value (5) into y. Output: x=7 y=5.
notes_text: The arrows in the diagram are crucial: they show that px contains 0x7bf0 (the address of main's x) and py contains 0x7bf4 (the address of main's y). When *px = *py executes, it reads the value at py's address (7) and writes it to px's address, which is main's x. This is the fundamental mechanism of pass-by-reference.

images.description: Completed stack diagram with arrows from *px to main's x and *py to main's y, showing x changing from 5 to 7 and y changing from 7 to 5 after the swap operations.

title: Correct Usage of Pointers - Multiply Example (Blank)
summary: Demonstrates correct pointer usage with a multiply function that returns results via pointer parameter instead of return value.
main_text: Commonly functions will take some inputs and produce some outputs. We'll use a simple 'multiply' function for now even though we can easily compute this without a function. We could use the return value but let's practice with pointers and say mul1() must return void. Pass a pointer to have one function modify the variable of another. Two versions: int mul1(int in1, int in2) { return in1 * in2; } uses a return value. void mul2(int in1, int in2, int* out) uses a pointer parameter. In main(): int wid = 8, len = 5, a; mul2(wid, len, ______); cout << "Ans. is " << a << endl; Students must fill in the call argument (&a) and the function body (*out = in1 * in2). The stack shows mul's frame with in1=8, in2=5, out=0x7bf8 (address of a in main), and main's a changes from garbage (-732) to 40.
notes_text: This pattern is common in C programming where functions need to return multiple values: pass pointers to output variables. The caller passes &a (address of a) as the third argument, and the callee writes the result through *out = in1 * in2. This is more flexible than return values because a function can have multiple output parameters.

images.description: Stack diagram showing mul's frame with in1=8, in2=5, out=0x7bf8, and main's frame with wid=8, len=5, a changing from -732 to 40. Blanks to be filled in the code.

title: Correct Usage of Pointers - Multiply Example (Solution)
summary: Shows the completed multiply example: mul2(wid, len, &a) passes address of a, and *out = in1 * in2 writes the result.
main_text: The completed solution: In main(): mul2(wid, len, &a); passes the address of a as the third argument. The function: void mul2(int in1, int in2, int* out) { *out = in1 * in2; } writes the product through the pointer. The stack shows mul's frame: in1=8 at 0x7be0, in2=5 at 0x7be4, out=0x7bf8 at 0x7be8 (address of main's a), return link at 0x7bec. Main's frame: wid=8 at 0x7bf0, len=5 at 0x7bf4, a changes from -732 to 40 at 0x7bf8. The dereference *out = in1 * in2 writes 40 directly into main's variable a.
notes_text: This pattern (passing output parameters by pointer) is the standard C idiom for functions that need to produce multiple results. In C++, references provide a cleaner syntax for the same purpose, but understanding the pointer-based approach is essential for C compatibility and for understanding how references work under the hood.

images.description: Stack diagram showing the completed mul2 example with out=0x7bf8 pointing to main's a, which changes from -732 to 40 after *out = in1 * in2 executes.

title: Misuse of Pointers - Returning Pointer to Dead Variable
summary: Warns against returning a pointer to a local variable, which becomes a dangling pointer after the function returns.
main_text: Make sure you don't return a pointer to a dead variable. Local variables of a function die when the function ends. If you return a pointer to a local variable of that function, BAD things happen! You might get lucky and find that old value still there, but likely you won't. Bad example: int* badmul1(int in1, int in2) { int out = in1 * in2; return &out; } In main(): int *a = badmul1(wid,len); cout << "Ans. is " << *a << endl; The problem: badmul1 computes out = 40 in its stack frame, then returns &out (address 0x7be0). But when badmul1 returns, its stack frame is deallocated. The pointer a now points to memory that is no longer valid (a dangling pointer). The value at that address may be overwritten by the next function call.
notes_text: This is one of the most dangerous pointer errors. The stack frame for badmul1 is reclaimed after it returns, so the address stored in a points to memory that could be reused by any subsequent function call. The behavior is undefined -- it might work sometimes and crash other times, making the bug extremely hard to track down. Never return the address of a local variable.

images.description: Stack diagram showing badmul1's frame with out=40 at 0x7be0, and main's a receiving 0x7be0 -- but after badmul1 returns, the memory at 0x7be0 is no longer valid.

title: Digging Deeper: Pointers are Passed-by-Value
summary: Clarifies that even pointers themselves are passed by value (a copy of the address is made), but the copy still allows access to the original data.
main_text: Notice that even pointers are PASSED-BY-VALUE! A copy of the address is sent to the function. But that copy of the address allows us to access the original variable! The pointer argument lives on the stack of the callee function. But it can be used (by dereferencing it) to access the local variable from the caller and modify its data. When the callee finishes and returns, the pointer argument dies, but the caller will now see the updated value of its local variable. Example: void dec(int); prototype. In main(): int y = 3; dec(&y); cout << y << endl; // prints 2. In dec(int* ptr): *ptr = *ptr - 1;. Stack shows: dec's ptr at 0x7bf0 holds 7bf8 (copy of y's address), and *ptr dereferences to access and modify main's y from 3 to 2.
notes_text: This is a subtle but important point: C/C++ ALWAYS passes by value. When we say 'pass-by-reference using pointers,' what actually happens is the ADDRESS is passed by value. The callee gets its own copy of the address, but since both copies of the address refer to the same memory location, dereferencing either copy accesses the same data. The pointer variable ptr is local to dec and will be destroyed when dec returns, but the modification to *ptr (which is main's y) persists.

images.description: Stack diagram showing dec's ptr at 0x7bf0 containing 7bf8 (a copy of the address of y), with *ptr arrow pointing to main's y at 0x7bf8, which changes from 3 to 2.

title: Pass-by-Reference Template
summary: Provides a general template for pass-by-reference: function takes T* parameter, caller passes &var, callee dereferences *varptr = value.
main_text: To modify a type T variable named var in another function: Set the function to take a T* varptr parameter. Pass &var in the caller function to create and send a pointer to the function. In the calling function, dereference the pointer and assign: *varptr = value. Basic Example: // here T = double. void f1(double* pvar) { *pvar = 3.9; } int main() { double var; f1(&var); cout << var << endl; return 0; }. Advanced Example (if time): // here T = int*. void f2(int dat[], int len, int** pptr) { int maxidx = 0; // loop to find the index of max; *pptr = &dat[maxidx]; } int main() { int dat[10] = { ... }; int* ptr; f2(dat, 10, &ptr); cout << "Max: " << *ptr << endl; return 0; }. The advanced example shows passing a pointer-to-pointer (int**) to modify an int* variable in the caller.
notes_text: The template is universal: for any type T, to modify a T variable in another function, pass T* and dereference with *. The advanced example extends this: to modify an int* variable (T = int*), pass int** (a pointer to a pointer). The caller passes &ptr (address of the pointer variable), and the callee writes *pptr = &dat[maxidx] to set ptr to point to the maximum element.

title: Pass-by-Reference Exercises - Section Header
summary: Section divider introducing practice exercises for pass-by-reference with pointers.
main_text: This is a section header introducing the Pass-by-Reference Exercises section. The following slides contain practice problems that test understanding of when to use & (address-of) vs passing directly, matching argument types to parameter types, and determining which variables can be modified by a function based on its signature.
notes_text: These exercises are critical for building fluency with pointer syntax. Students must practice identifying when & is needed (for scalar pass-by-reference) vs. when it is not (for arrays, which are already passed by reference).

title: Exercise Set 1 - Completing Function Calls
summary: Practice exercise: given function signatures, students must fill in the correct arguments (with or without &) in function calls.
main_text: Consider the functions shown on the left and their signatures. Complete the function calls in main() by filling in the appropriate arguments. Functions: void f1(int* a, double b) { /* not shown */ }; void f2(int a, string* b) { /* not shown */ }; void f3(char* a, double* b) { /* not shown */ }; void f4(string a, char b) { /* not shown */ }. In main(): char w[6] = "hello"; int x = 5; double y = 2.5; string z = "bye"; f1(______, ______); /* pass x */ /* pass y */. f2(______, ______); /* pass x */ /* pass z */. f3(______, ______); /* pass w */ /* pass y */. f4(______, ______); /* pass z */ /* pass 'e' in "hello" */. Students must determine when to use & based on whether the parameter type is a pointer.
notes_text: The key rule: if the parameter type is T*, you must pass the address using &variable for scalars, or just the array name for arrays. If the parameter type is T (no *), you pass the variable directly. For f1: int* a requires &x, double b takes y directly. For f3: char* a can take w directly (array name is a pointer), double* b requires &y.

title: Exercise Set 2 - True/False on Variable Modification
summary: Practice exercise: determine whether functions can modify specific caller variables based on pass-by-value vs pass-by-reference parameters.
main_text: Consider the functions shown on the left and their signatures. Given the code in main(), answer the T/F questions for each function call. Functions: void f1(int a, double b) { /* not shown */ }; void f2(int a, string* b) { /* not shown */ }; void f3(char a[], double* b) { /* not shown */ }; void f4(int* a, char b) { /* not shown */ }. In main(): char w[6] = "hello"; int x = 5; double y = 2.5; string z = "bye"; Q1 (T/F): f1() can change x and y. Q2 (T/F): f2() can change z but not x. Q3 (T/F): f3() can change y but not w. Q4 (T/F): f4() can change x and w[1]. Students must analyze each parameter type to determine if it allows modification of the original variable.
notes_text: The analysis: f1(int a, double b) -- both pass-by-value, cannot change either x or y. f2(int a, string* b) -- a is by value (can't change x), b is pointer (can change z). f3(char a[], double* b) -- a[] is array/pointer (can change w), b is pointer (can change y). f4(int* a, char b) -- a is pointer (can change x), b is by value (can't change w[1]).

title: Exercise Set 3 - Writing Function Signatures and Calls
summary: Advanced exercise: given tasks in main(), students must write both the function signatures and the function calls.
main_text: Given the tasks in main(), complete the function signatures and function calls. In main(): char w[6] = "hello"; int x = 5; double y = 2.5; string z = "bye"; Call f1() to change y but only use x and w: f1(______, ______); Call f2() to change w and z: f2(______, ______); Call f3() to change the 'e' in hello, change x, but only use y: f3(______, ______); Students must also write the corresponding function prototypes: void f1(______); void f2(______); void f3(______). This requires reasoning about which parameters need to be pointers (to allow modification) and which can be passed by value.
notes_text: This exercise requires students to work backwards: from the desired behavior (which variables need to change), determine the parameter types (T* for modifiable, T for read-only). For f1: y needs to change (double*), x is read-only (int), w is an array (char*). For f2: w needs to change (char*), z needs to change (string*). For f3: w[1] needs to change (char*), x needs to change (int*), y is read-only (double).

title: Exercise Set 1 Solution
summary: Solution to Exercise Set 1: f1(&x, y), f2(x, &z), f3(w, &y), f4(z, w[1]).
main_text: Solutions for the function calls: f1(&x, y); -- int* a requires &x (address of x), double b takes y directly. f2(x, &z); -- int a takes x directly, string* b requires &z (address of z). f3(w, &y); -- char* a takes w directly (array name is already a pointer), double* b requires &y (address of y). f4(z, w[1]); -- string a takes z directly, char b takes w[1] directly (a single char from the array). Key insight: arrays are already pointers so no & is needed, but scalar variables need & when the parameter is a pointer type.
notes_text: Common mistakes: (1) Using &w for f3 when w already evaluates to a pointer. (2) Forgetting & for scalar pointers like &x in f1 or &z in f2. (3) For f4, w[1] is a char value ('e'), not an address, which matches the char b parameter.

title: Exercise Set 2 Solution
summary: Solution: Q1 False (can change neither), Q2 True, Q3 False (can change both), Q4 False (can change x but not w[1]).
main_text: Solutions: Q1 (T/F): f1(int a, double b) can change x and y -- FALSE. Can change neither. Both parameters are pass-by-value, so neither x nor y can be modified. Q2 (T/F): f2(int a, string* b) can change z but not x -- TRUE. string* b allows changing z, int a is by value so x cannot change. Q3 (T/F): f3(char a[], double* b) can change y but not w -- FALSE. Can change both. char a[] is an array parameter (pass-by-reference), so w CAN be changed. double* b also allows changing y. Q4 (T/F): f4(int* a, char b) can change x and w[1] -- FALSE. Can change x but not w[1]. int* a allows changing x, but char b is pass-by-value, so w[1] cannot be changed.
notes_text: The key analysis technique: for each parameter, check if the type includes * or []. If yes, the original variable can be modified (pass-by-reference). If no, it cannot (pass-by-value). Note that char a[] and char* a are equivalent as function parameters -- both allow modification of the original array.

title: Exercise Set 3 Solution
summary: Solution showing function signatures and calls: f1(double*, int, char*), f2(char*, string*), f3(char*, int*, double).
main_text: Solutions: void f1(double* a, int x, char* w) -- to change y, need double*; x is read-only (int); w is an array (char*). Call: f1(&y, x, w); void f2(char* w, string* b) -- to change w, char* (array already a pointer); to change z, string*. Call: f2(w, &z); void f3(char* a, int* b, double c) -- to change the 'e' in hello, need char* pointing to that element; to change x, int*; y is read-only (double). Call: f3(&w[1], &x, y); Note for f3: &w[1] gives the address of the second character in the array, which is 'e'. This allows f3 to modify that specific character.
notes_text: The most challenging part is f3: passing &w[1] to modify a specific character in the array. This demonstrates that you can take the address of any array element, not just the entire array. Also note that the order of parameters in the function signature is a design choice -- the key is matching the types to the intended behavior (pointer for modifiable, value for read-only).

title: Pointer Arithmetic and Arrays - Section Header
summary: Section divider introducing Pointer Arithmetic and Arrays. Prerequisites: Pointer Basics, Data Sizes.
main_text: This section header introduces Pointer Arithmetic and Arrays. Prerequisites for this section are Pointer Basics and Data Sizes. The upcoming slides will cover how pointers and arrays are interchangeable, how pointer arithmetic works with type-based scaling, and how array indexing is equivalent to pointer arithmetic plus dereferencing.
notes_text: Understanding data sizes (int = 4 bytes, double = 8 bytes, char = 1 byte) is essential because pointer arithmetic implicitly scales by the size of the type being pointed to. This section connects pointers to arrays, showing they are two views of the same underlying mechanism.

title: Review Questions on Data Sizes and Arrays
summary: Review questions about int and double sizes, contiguous array storage, and calculating element addresses.
main_text: Review questions to test prerequisite knowledge: The size of an 'int' is how many bytes? (Answer: 4). The size of a 'double' is how many bytes? (Answer: 8). T/F: The elements of an array are stored contiguously in memory (Answer: True). In an array of integers, if dat[0] lived at address 0x200, dat[1] would live at...? (Answer: 0x204, because each int is 4 bytes, so the next element is 4 bytes later). These concepts are essential for understanding pointer arithmetic.
notes_text: These foundational facts drive pointer arithmetic: when you add 1 to an int*, the actual address increases by sizeof(int) = 4 bytes. When you add 1 to a double*, the address increases by sizeof(double) = 8 bytes. Contiguous storage means elements are stored one after another with no gaps, which is what makes pointer arithmetic work for traversing arrays.

title: Big Idea: Array Names and Pointers are Interchangeable
summary: Key concept: array names evaluate to pointers to the first element, and pointers can be used with array syntax.
main_text: Big idea: Array names and pointers are interchangeable. An array name is a pointer and a pointer can be used as an array name! Why? Because an array name by itself evaluates to the starting address of the first element. Given the declaration int dat[10], dat is an int* (type). Given the declaration char str[6], str is a char* (type). A pointer (i.e. int* ptr;) can be used as an array name once you point it to some location. Example: int dat[5] = {10,11,12,13,14}; *dat = 1; // array name as ptr: same as dat[0] = 1. int *p = dat; // array name as ptr: same as int* p = &dat[0]. p[1] = p[2]-8; // ptr as array name: same as dat[1]=dat[2]-8. This is possible through pointer arithmetic.
notes_text: This is one of the most important concepts in C/C++: arrays and pointers are deeply connected. The array name 'decays' to a pointer to its first element in most contexts. This means dat and &dat[0] are equivalent, and p[i] and *(p+i) are equivalent. This duality is what makes C arrays flexible but also potentially confusing.

title: A Logical Progression to Pointer Arithmetic
summary: Builds the logical argument: pointers store addresses, addresses are numbers, numbers support arithmetic, therefore pointers support arithmetic.
main_text: Consider the logical progression: Pointers are variables storing addresses. Addresses are just numbers. We can perform arithmetic on numbers. Therefore, we should be able to perform arithmetic on pointers! This chain of reasoning motivates why pointer arithmetic exists and is a natural extension of the concept of pointers as address-storing variables.
notes_text: This slide provides the logical foundation for pointer arithmetic. While the reasoning is simple, the implementation has an important twist: pointer arithmetic is scaled by the size of the type being pointed to. Adding 1 to a pointer does not add 1 to the address; it adds sizeof(pointed-to-type) to the address. This scaling is what makes pointer arithmetic useful for traversing arrays.

title: Pointer Arithmetic with int Arrays
summary: Explains pointer arithmetic: adding/subtracting from pointers is scaled by sizeof(type), so ptr+1 advances by one element, not one byte.
main_text: We can perform addition or subtraction on pointer variables (i.e. addresses) just like any other variable. This is known as pointer arithmetic. Important Difference: The number added/subtracted is implicitly scaled (multiplied) by the size of the type pointed to, ensuring the resulting address points to a valid data item. Example with int dat[6] and int* ptr = &dat[2] (ptr = 73a8): ptr+1 points to dat[3] at 73a8+1*4 = 73ac. ptr+2 points to dat[4] at 73a8+2*4 = 73b0. ptr-1 points to dat[1] at 73a8-1*4 = 73a4. ptr-2 points to dat[0] at 73a8-2*4 = 73a0. The scaling by sizeof(int) = 4 ensures each arithmetic step moves exactly one int element forward or backward in the array.
notes_text: The implicit scaling is the key insight: the compiler knows the type of the pointer and automatically multiplies the offset by sizeof(type). This means ptr+1 always means 'the next element' regardless of the element size, which makes pointer arithmetic intuitive for array traversal. Without scaling, programmers would have to manually compute byte offsets.

title: Pointer Arithmetic with double and char Arrays
summary: Shows pointer arithmetic scaling for double* (adds 8 bytes per step) compared to int* (adds 4 bytes per step).
main_text: Pointer arithmetic implicit scales the added value based on the type of pointer. For an int*, adding +2 really adds +2 * sizeof(int) = +2*4 = 8 so that the pointer will point 2 integers away. For a double*, adding +2 really adds +2 * sizeof(double) = +2*8 = 16 so that the pointer will point 2 doubles away. Example: double gpa[6] with values {3.5, 2.9, 3.7, 3.9, 2.6, 3.2} starting at address 73a0. double* p2 = gpa+2 (p2 = 73b0, pointing to gpa[2]). p2+1 = 73b0+1*8 = 73b8 (gpa[3]). p2-1 = 73b0-1*8 = 73a8 (gpa[1]). Each step is 8 bytes because sizeof(double) = 8.
notes_text: Comparing the two diagrams makes the scaling crystal clear: for int arrays, each step is 4 bytes; for double arrays, each step is 8 bytes. The programmer writes the same code (ptr+1, ptr+2) regardless of type -- the compiler handles the scaling automatically. This type-based scaling is what makes pointer arithmetic type-safe and portable across different architectures.

images.description: Diagram showing double gpa[6] array in memory from 73a0 to 73c8, with each element 8 bytes apart. double* p2 points to gpa[2] at 73b0. Shows p2-2 through p2+3 positions with byte calculations.

title: Pointer Arithmetic with char Arrays
summary: Shows pointer arithmetic for char*: adding +2 adds only 2 bytes since sizeof(char) = 1.
main_text: Pointer arithmetic implicit scales the added value based on the type of pointer. For a char*, adding +2 really adds +2 * sizeof(char) = +2*1 = 2 so that the pointer will point 2 chars away. Example: char ltr[6] with values {'a','b','c','d','e','f'} starting at address 73a0. char* p3 = ltr+2 (p3 = 73a2, pointing to ltr[2] which is 'c'). p3+1 = 73a2+1*1 = 73a3 (ltr[3], 'd'). p3-1 = 73a2-1*1 = 73a1 (ltr[1], 'b'). Each step is just 1 byte because sizeof(char) = 1. For char pointers, the arithmetic offset equals the byte offset since each char is exactly 1 byte.
notes_text: The char* case is the simplest: since sizeof(char) = 1, pointer arithmetic and byte arithmetic are identical. This is why char* is often used for raw byte manipulation in C/C++. Comparing all three types: int* moves 4 bytes per step, double* moves 8 bytes per step, and char* moves 1 byte per step.

images.description: Diagram showing char ltr[6] array in memory from 73a0 to 73a5, with each element 1 byte apart. char* p3 points to ltr[2] at 73a2. Shows p3-2 through p3+3 with simple byte calculations.

title: Pointer Arithmetic and Array Indexing Equivalence
summary: Demonstrates that *(data + i) is equivalent to data[i], connecting pointer arithmetic to array indexing.
main_text: Pointer arithmetic and array indexing are really the same! Pointer syntax vs. Array syntax: *(data + i) <=> data[i]. (data + i) computes the address of the i-th value in an array and the * operator gets its value. Example: int data[6] = {10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15} starting at address 73a0. int* ptr = data (ptr = 73a0, same as &data[0]). *(data + 0) = data[0] = 10 at 73a0. *(data + 1) = data[1] = 11 at 73a4. *(ptr + 2) = ptr[2] = data[2] = 12 at 73a8. The diagram shows both the data/ptr offset notation and the corresponding array index notation, demonstrating they produce identical results.
notes_text: This equivalence is fundamental to C/C++: the bracket operator [] is syntactic sugar for pointer arithmetic plus dereference. data[i] is literally defined as *(data + i). This means you can use either notation interchangeably. The diagram shows both notations side by side to reinforce the equivalence.

images.description: Diagram showing int data[6] array with both array index labels (data[0] through data[5]) and pointer offset labels (ptr[0]/data+0 through ptr+5). int* ptr points to data[0] at 73a0. The formula *(data + i) <=> data[i] is highlighted.

title: Pointer Arithmetic and Array Indexing Examples
summary: Demonstrates interchangeable use of pointer and array syntax: pointers with [] and array names with * and pointer arithmetic.
main_text: Pointer arithmetic and array indexing are really the same! Pointer syntax vs. Array syntax: *(data + i) <=> data[i]. We can use pointers and array names interchangeably (an array name is a pointer and a pointer can be treated as an array name and [] applied). Examples: int data[6] = {10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15}; // data = 73a0. *(data + 4) = 50; // treat data like a pointer and perform data[4] = 50. int* ptr = data; // ptr now points at 73a0 too. ptr[1] = ptr[2] + ptr[3]; // treat ptr like array name (same as data[1]=data[2]+data[3]). After these operations: data[4] changes from 14 to 50, and data[1] changes from 11 to 25 (12+13).
notes_text: The examples demonstrate bidirectional interchangeability: an array name can be used with * and pointer arithmetic (*(data + 4) = 50), and a pointer can be used with [] (ptr[1] = ptr[2] + ptr[3]). This flexibility is a defining feature of C/C++ that other languages generally do not provide.

images.description: Array diagram showing int data[6] with both data and ptr labels, showing values updating: data[4] from 14 to 50, data[1] from 11 to 25.

title: Arrays vs Pointers - Three Equivalent Initialization Methods
summary: Shows three equivalent ways to initialize an array using pointers: common array syntax, explicit pointer arithmetic, and walking pointer.
main_text: All 3 methods below perform the same task of initializing the array. Which do you prefer? Remember, your goal is to make your code readable (option 1) but you should understand all 3. Method 1 - Common Array Syntax: int dat[10]; int *ptr1 = dat; for(int i=0; i < 10; i++) { ptr1[i] = 0; // equivalent to dat[i] = 0; }. Method 2 - Explicit pointer arithmetic: int dat[10]; int *ptr2 = dat; for(int i=0; i < 10; i++) { *(ptr2+i) = 0; }. Method 3 - Walking Pointer: int dat[10]; int *ptr3 = dat; for(int i=0; i < 10; i++) { *ptr3 = 0; ptr3++; }. The walking pointer method increments the pointer itself after each use, so it moves through the array element by element.
notes_text: Option 1 (array syntax with pointer) is the most readable and preferred in practice. Option 2 (explicit arithmetic) makes the pointer math visible. Option 3 (walking pointer) is a common C idiom but modifies the pointer variable, which means ptr3 no longer points to the beginning of the array after the loop. All three produce identical machine code. The walking pointer pattern is common in string processing with char*.

main_text: The number added/subtracted to the pointer is implicitly scaled (multiplied) by the size of the type pointed to, ensuring the resulting address points to a valid data item. Given: int dat[] = {103, 5, 1}; int len=0; double gpa[3] = {3.7, 3.5, 3.1}; int *ptr1 = dat; double *ptr2 = gpa; Memory layout shown with dat at 73a0, len at 73ac, gpa at 73b0, ptr1 at 73c8, ptr2 at 73cc. Students fill in the blanks.

The final 'What if??' question asks what happens if you dereference a pointer that has gone past the end of its array -- this is undefined behavior.

title: Pointer Arithmetic Examples (Solution)
summary: Completed solution showing pointer arithmetic tracing with filled-in byte offsets and updated memory values.
main_text: Completed tracing: *ptr1 = 104; // dat[0] changes from 103 to 104, ptr1 still at 73a0. ptr1 = ptr1 + 2; // addr. inc. by 2*4=8 (2*sizeof(int)), ptr1 goes from 73a0 to 73a8. The final // *ptr2 = 2.9; question: ptr2 now points past the end of the gpa array into ptr1's memory -- writing here would corrupt ptr1's value. This is undefined behavior.
notes_text: The *ptr2++ = 4.0 expression uses C++ operator precedence: the postfix ++ has higher precedence than *, but the increment happens after the entire expression is evaluated. So *ptr2 = 4.0 happens first, then ptr2 is incremented. After this, ptr2 points to address 73c8 which is the int* ptr1 variable -- dereferencing and writing here would overwrite ptr1 with a double bit pattern, causing data corruption.

title: Recall: Passing Arrays as Arguments
summary: Reviews how arrays are passed to functions: formal parameter uses type[] or type*, actual argument is just the array name.
main_text: In function declaration / prototype for the formal parameter use type [] or type * to indicate an array is being passed. Both are equivalent: int sum(int data[], int size); or int sum(int* data, int size);. When calling the function, simply provide the name of the array as the actual argument. In C/C++ using an array name without any index evaluates to the starting address of the array (a pointer to the 0th element). Example: int sum(int data[], int size) { int total = 0; for(int i=0; i < size; i++) { total += data[i]; } return total; } int main() { int vals[100]; /* some code to initialize vals */ int mysum = sum(vals, 100); cout << mysum << endl; return 0; }. Recall: To access an element in an array, we need 3 pieces of info: 1. Start address of the array, 2. Index/offset, 3. Type of elements in the array (really the size of that type).
notes_text: The three pieces of information (start address, index, type/size) are exactly what pointer arithmetic uses: address + index * sizeof(type). The function parameter int data[] and int* data are completely interchangeable -- the compiler treats them identically. The array name vals evaluates to a pointer (address 7420 in the example) when passed to the function.

images.description: Code example showing sum function with int data[] parameter and main calling sum(vals, 100), with a callout noting the three pieces of info needed to access array elements.

title: Stack View of Passing Arrays
summary: Shows the stack memory layout when passing arrays, demonstrating that the array name evaluates to an int* address.
main_text: Main point: A pointer and an array name are interchangeable! The stack diagram shows what happens when sum(vals, 100) is called. sum's stack frame: i (loop counter cycling 0,1,...99,100), total starts at 0 and accumulates to 500, data = 7420 (the starting address of vals in main), size = 100, return link. main's stack frame: mysum = 500, vals[0] through vals[99] all containing 5, return link. The key observation: data in sum's frame holds 7420, which is the address of vals[0]. Inside sum, data[i] is equivalent to *(data+i), which computes 7420 + i*4 to access each element. The annotation shows vals is 'An int*' -- the array name evaluates to a pointer. The alternative function signature int sum(int* data, int size) would work identically.
notes_text: This stack diagram clearly shows the mechanism: when vals is passed to sum, only its address (7420) is copied into sum's data parameter. The entire 100-element array is NOT copied -- only the 8-byte address is passed. This is efficient (only 8 bytes instead of 400 bytes) and allows sum to access and potentially modify the original array data.

title: One or Many - Pointer Ambiguity
summary: Explains that C/C++ cannot distinguish whether a pointer points to a single variable or an array; only context and documentation clarify this.
main_text: Strange question: Is 3240 McClintock Ave. the address of a single-family house or a large dormitory with many suites? We can't know from the address alone. In the same way, C/C++ does not differentiate whether a pointer points to a single variable or an array (i.e. it doesn't have additional syntax). It can only be determined based on how the function uses the pointer (does it treat the pointer as being to an array OR to a single value). Good commenting/documentation should describe this. Example 1 - Pointer to a single variable: void f1(int* p) { *p -= 1; } // f1 decrements the integer pointed to by p. Example 2 - Pointer to an array: void f1(int* p) { for(int i=0; i < 10; i++) { p[i] = 0; } } // f1 sets the array pointed to by p to all zeros. Both functions have identical signatures but treat p completely differently.
notes_text: This is a fundamental limitation of C/C++ that does not exist in higher-level languages with proper array types. The programmer must know from documentation or context whether a pointer refers to a single element or an array. This ambiguity is a common source of bugs. Modern C++ prefers std::array or std::vector which carry their size information, avoiding this ambiguity.

title: const or non-const Pointers
summary: Introduces the const modifier for pointers: const prevents modification, acting like 'Can View' vs 'Can Edit' permissions.
main_text: The const modifier on a variable type means it may not be modified or changed after being initialized. Why would we want that? Because YOU are your OWN WORST ENEMY when programming! You make mistakes. The more we can enlist the compiler to help us catch mistakes, the better. If our intention is for a variable not to change, then declare it const. Example: const int size = 5; size = 6; // Compile Error. A const pointer means we can dereference the pointer to GET (view) the data but NOT use the pointer to CHANGE (edit) the data. Similar to 'Can View' vs. 'Can Edit' permission on a Google doc. Non-const: void f1(int* p, int size) { for(int i=0; i < size; i++) { p[i] = 0; } } // Can modify array (Editor). Const: void f1(const int* p, int size) { for(int i=0; i < size; i++) { cout << p[i] << endl; p[i] = 0; // compile error } } // Cannot modify array (Viewer).
notes_text: The const modifier is a powerful tool for bug prevention. By marking pointers as const when modification is not intended, the compiler catches accidental writes at compile time rather than letting them cause bugs at runtime. The Google Doc analogy (Editor = non-const, Viewer = const) maps perfectly to this concept.

title: Const or Non-Const Example
summary: Shows when to mark array parameters as const: init() modifies the array (no const), sum() only reads it (use const).
main_text: Which parameters of the functions should be marked as const? Does size need to be marked const? No! Since it is already a copy (pass-by-value), marking it const provides no benefit to the caller. Would it make sense to try to mark an email attachment as 'view only'? No! Since it is already a copy. For init(): void init(int data[], int size) -- data should NOT be const because init writes to the array (cin >> data[i]). Alternatively: void init(int* data, int size). For sum(): int sum(const int data[], int size) -- data SHOULD be const because sum only reads from the array (total += data[i]). Alternatively: int sum(const int* data, int size). The annotation shows vals (the array name) is 'An int*' when passed to either function. Using const for sum's parameter signals to both the compiler and the reader that sum will not modify the array.
notes_text: The key insight about pass-by-value parameters (like size): adding const to them does not protect the caller since they are copies anyway. Const is most valuable for pointer/reference parameters where it protects the caller's original data. In practice, functions that only read data through a pointer should always use const -- this is a strong signal of intent and enables the compiler to catch accidental modifications.

title: C String Function Library (<cstring>)
summary: Introduces the C string library functions: strlen, strcmp, strcpy, strcat, and strchr, all operating on char* pointers.
main_text: A library of functions was provided to perform operations on these character arrays representing strings (<cstring> in C++, <string.h> in C). int strlen(const char *dest) / int strlen(const char dest[]) -- returns the length of the string. int strcmp(const char *str1, const char *str2); -- returns 0 if equal, >0 if first non-equal char in str1 is alphanumerically larger, <0 otherwise. char *strcpy(char *dest, const char *src); -- copies src string into dest. char *strcat(char *dest, const char *src); -- concatenates src to the end of dest. char *strchr(const char *str, char c); -- finds first occurrence of character 'c' in str returning a pointer to that character or NULL if the character is not found. Notice the use of const: source/read-only parameters are marked const, while destination/modifiable parameters are not.
notes_text: These C string functions demonstrate all the pointer concepts covered in this unit: const correctness (const for read-only parameters, non-const for writable destinations), pointers as function parameters, and return values as pointers (strchr returns a pointer into the string). These functions operate on null-terminated character arrays (C-strings), which are the original string type before C++ std::string. Understanding these functions reinforces pointer concepts and is still relevant for systems programming.
